chapters.title: Chapter 8: Careers and the Business of Market Making in India

lessons.title: What a Market Making Desk Actually Hires For: Roles and Skills

body.text: A market making desk is not one job. It is a small pipeline of distinct roles, each one responsible for a different piece of the machinery this course has spent eight chapters building.

children.text: Quant Researcher: Building the Pricing Model

The quant researcher's job is essentially Chapters 2 through 4 of this course, made concrete and continuously recalibrated. This role designs the reservation price and spread logic from Avellaneda-Stoikov, estimates the risk aversion, volatility, and order-flow-sensitivity parameters those formulas actually need, and builds and maintains the adverse selection detection covered through PIN and VPIN. The work is fundamentally statistical: probability, historical data analysis, and enough comfort with the underlying mathematics to know when a model's assumptions are being stretched too far by real market conditions, exactly as Chapter 3's disclaimer on the Avellaneda-Stoikov model's own assumptions described.
Quant Developer: Building the System That Executes It

A pricing model is only as good as the system that turns it into real orders fast enough to matter. This role is Chapter 5 made real: building the order management system that sends the cancel-and-replace messages covered in that chapter's first lesson, optimising for the latency stack covered in the second, and implementing the pre-trade risk checks and kill switch required by SEBI's algorithmic trading framework from the third. This work leans heavily on systems programming, typically in languages built for speed and predictable performance, along with a genuine understanding of networking and hardware, since colocation and low-latency infrastructure are engineering problems as much as trading ones.
Trader and Risk Manager: Making the Judgment Calls

Not every decision in this course can be left entirely to a model. Someone has to set the risk limits that trigger an escalation from passive skewing to an aggressive unwind, exactly the judgment call worked through in Chapter 3's case study, and someone has to watch the operational metrics from Chapter 6, spread capture rate, fill ratio, drawdown, to decide whether a bad stretch reflects normal stress or a genuine problem with the model itself. At smaller firms this role often sits with the same person who oversees the quant research; at larger ones it can be a distinct seat responsible for real-time oversight and intervention across several desks at once.
Compliance and Data Roles: The Less Visible but Essential Work

Two further roles rarely get the same attention as pricing and speed, but neither is optional. Compliance and regulatory operations staff handle the unique algo ID registration, order-to-trade ratio monitoring, and kill switch testing obligations from Chapter 5, work that keeps the entire desk legally able to operate. Data and infrastructure staff maintain the historical tick data pipelines that quant researchers rely on to estimate PIN, backtest spread capture, and validate every model this course has covered, since none of that analysis is possible without clean, reliable, well-organised market data in the first place.

body.caption: Roles on a market making desk, mapped back to this course

cells: Pricing model, parameter estimation, adverse selection detection
Statistics, probability, applied mathematics, data analysis
Order execution system, latency optimisation, risk controls
Real-time oversight, risk limits, escalation decisions
Judgment under pressure, strategy fluency, risk intuition
Algo registration, OTR monitoring, kill switch testing
Tick data pipelines, historical data for research and backtesting

body.text: Smaller firms frequently blend several of these roles into one person, especially quant research and trading, or quant development and infrastructure. Larger, more established operations tend to separate them into genuinely distinct seats. Understanding which of these responsibilities most excites you matters more, at this stage, than trying to guess a specific firm's org chart.

body.title: Two Different Strengths
body.scenario: One candidate has a strong background in statistics and probability, has worked through this course's mathematical content comfortably, but has limited experience writing production-quality, high-performance code. Another candidate is an excellent systems programmer with real experience optimising for latency, but finds the statistical estimation content in Chapters 3 and 4 considerably harder going.
body.prompt: Which role from this lesson is the more natural starting point for each candidate, and why would it be a mistake for either of them to force themselves into the other's strongest-fit role right away?
body.modelAnswer: The first candidate is a more natural fit for a quant researcher track, where the statistical and probabilistic skills this course emphasised in Chapters 2 through 4 are the core of the job, even without strong systems programming experience yet. The second candidate is a more natural fit for a quant developer track, where systems programming and latency optimisation from Chapter 5 are the central skill, even without deep comfort in the statistical estimation methods. Forcing either candidate into the other's strongest-fit role risks a weak match on day one: the first candidate would struggle disproportionately with the low-latency engineering demands, and the second would struggle disproportionately with correctly estimating and validating a pricing model's parameters, when each already has a clear, more natural entry point into the same overall business.

body.title: Where Compliance Work Actually Sits
body.question: Which chapter's content is most directly the responsibility of a market making desk's compliance and regulatory operations staff?
options: Chapter 5's algorithmic trading obligations, including unique algo IDs, order-to-trade ratio monitoring, and kill switches
body.explanation: Compliance and regulatory operations staff are specifically responsible for keeping the desk within SEBI's algorithmic trading framework, covered in Chapter 5, including algo registration, order-to-trade ratio monitoring, and kill switch testing. The other listed topics belong more directly to the quant researcher and trader roles covered earlier in this lesson.

points: A quant researcher role centres on Chapters 2 through 4's pricing and adverse selection content, and leans heavily on statistics and probability
A quant developer role centres on Chapter 5's execution and latency content, and leans heavily on systems programming and infrastructure
A trader or risk manager role makes the real-time judgment calls from Chapters 3 and 6, escalation decisions and metric interpretation under live conditions
Compliance and data infrastructure roles are less visible but essential, keeping the desk regulatorily compliant and supplying the clean data every other role depends on
Smaller firms often blend these roles together, while larger firms tend to separate them into distinct seats
The next lesson turns to how candidates for these roles actually get hired in practice
